receiving.title: Procurement 6 — Purchase Receipts & Quality: Goods In
receiving.desc: The receiving gate: receipt anatomy, count-before-sign discipline, serial and batch identities born at the gate, rejections and quality inspection with quarantine, landed-cost mechanics, returns to supplier, and the three gate rules.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Purchase Receipt, field by field
lessons.html:
Selling 5 taught that the Delivery Note is where the system's word meets the world, outbound. The Purchase Receipt is the same gate facing the other way — the document standing at the dock when goods ARRIVE, whose submission moves stock IN and writes valuation. Everything the firm will later sell, count, and cost enters through this document, and its craft decides whether the warehouse's truth starts true.

  • Supplier and the PO link — created FROM the Purchase Order (Chapter 2's discipline), inheriting supplier, items, rates, and target warehouses; the PO's fulfilment ledger counts down as this document submits.
  • Posting date and time — when possession was actually taken. The stock ledger is a chronology inbound exactly as outbound: valuation, stock-as-at, and every dispute read this date as fact, and Chapter 9 convicts the batching habit that fictionalises it.
  • The items grid — per row: item, the quantity in the PO's UOM with its conversion (Buying 2's arithmetic at the moment it becomes bins — 180 Carton-12 entering as 2,160 units), the rate travelling from the PO, and TWO quantity fields that selling's gate never needed: Accepted Qty into the target warehouse, and Rejected Qty into a rejected warehouse — the quality fork built into the document itself (Chapter 4 owns it).
  • Serial and batch sections — for tracked items, identities are ENTERED here: this is where serials and batches are BORN into your system (Chapter 3 — arguably the most consequential data-entry moment in the entire trading cycle).
  • Supplier document references — their delivery note number, waybill, container and seal numbers for imports: the fields that tie your receipt to their paper, worth thirty seconds at the gate and hours in any later dispute.

What submission does — and its weight. Accepted quantities enter their warehouses; rejected quantities enter quarantine; valuation is written — the received stock carries cost from the PO's rates (completed by landed charges where they apply, Chapter 5), and that valuation is what flows to cost-of-goods when selling ships it and what margin reports subtract forever. The receipt is thus not warehouse paperwork; it is the birth certificate of every unit's cost and identity. Draft, check against the physical count and the PO, then submit — because inbound, exactly as outbound, submission is the first irreversible moment, and unwinding it is a real operation (cancellation while untouched; a formal return, Chapter 6, once reality has moved on).

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The receiving discipline
lessons.html:
The gate is the last CHEAP moment of truth in the inbound chain: after it, every error costs a document trail to unwind; before it, errors cost a recount. This chapter is the discipline that spends the cheap moment well.

Create from the PO — the spine's inbound landing. The receipt is made FROM the Purchase Order: rows pre-fill with the exact remaining quantities (the remainder machinery you know — a second drop pre-fills at what drop one left, never at the original total, never from memory), rates travel untouched, target warehouses arrive as planned, and the PO's received-percentage advances itself. The from-scratch receipt is Procurement 5's Pattern 2 committed at the dock: real stock moved, ledger orphaned, the three-way match disarmed before it ever runs.

Count before sign — the physical half of the match. The three-way match (Procurement 7 completes it) has three legs: what was ORDERED (the PO), what was RECEIVED (this document), what was INVOICED (theirs). This chapter's leg is the physical one, and its integrity is simple and absolute: the receipt records what was actually counted, not what the paperwork says arrived. The sequence: the truck's contents counted against the PO (not against the supplier's delivery note — theirs says what they claim they sent; the PO says what you ordered; the count says what came); discrepancies recorded AS the receipt's quantities (short is short, damaged is rejected — Chapter 4); and only then the supplier's paper signed, annotated with any variance. Signing clean and sorting it out later converts your evidence into their receipt.

Partial receipts. Deliveries split — Emzor's two drops, the import that clears in stages. Each arrival is its own receipt from the PO at its actual quantities; the PO tracks the accumulating received-percentage; the remainder stays visibly open (Partially Received) until delivered or short-closed (Procurement 5's Close discipline). Nothing about partiality requires side-lists: the PO's arithmetic is the authority, drop after drop.

Receiving speaks the PO's units. The UOM drill from Buying 2, at its moment: the receipt enters quantities in the PO row's unit, and the conversion counts the ledger — 47 cartons and 6 loose units is two honest rows, never 47.5, never re-keyed piece-counts into carton rows. The factor-of-twelve disease is born at this desk or nowhere.

Submission follows the count. The document is completed AFTER the physical verification, recording what was gathered in — never submitted from the truck's manifest and corrected later, which is the ledger dictating fiction first and confessing after (Selling 5's conviction, verbatim, inbound). At a busy dock the discipline costs minutes; its absence costs stocktakes.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Serial & batch identities: born at this gate
lessons.html:
Selling 5 taught the recall drill and the serial disciplines — reading identities OUT. This chapter is where those identities come FROM: every serial and every batch in your system is born on a Purchase Receipt, and the quality of that birth decides whether the outbound disciplines can exist at all.

Serials at receipt. An item flagged Has Serial No demands, on the receipt row, the exact serial numbers arriving — keyed or scanned from the physical units. From this moment each unit has a biography the system can write: received on this document, from this supplier, at this cost, on this date; then its life through stock, delivery, warranty, and return. The craft point that decides everything downstream: capture from the units, not from the supplier's packing list — lists lie (repacks, substitutions, transcription), and a serial recorded that never physically arrived is a ghost that surfaces as Selling 5's impossible-return years later. Scan-driven capture where barcodes exist; careful physical keying where they do not; never bulk-pasted paperwork.

Batches at receipt — with the expiry. A batched item's receipt records WHICH lot arrived and — the field that carries regulatory weight — its expiry date, read from the physical cartons. This entry is the foundation of everything Selling 5 promised: FEFO picking exists only if expiries were captured truthfully; the NAFDAC recall drill (which customers received batch B-204?) is answerable in minutes only because this desk recorded B-204 when it arrived; and shelf-life management (refusing goods arriving with unacceptably short dating — a standing receiving rule for pharma: minimum remaining shelf life per the firm's policy, goods under it rejected at the gate, Chapter 4's fork) begins with reading the carton. The full provenance chain now closes: supplier batch documentation (Procurement 1's onboarding gate) → batch captured at receipt → batch on every outbound DN → recall answerable in both directions: which customers got it, AND which supplier sent it.

The two-sided recall. Walk it once, whole: the regulator names batch B-204. Outbound: DNs filtered by batch — customers, branches, quantities, dates (Selling 5's drill). Inbound: the receipt that brought B-204 names the supplier, the PO, the date, and the supplier's own batch paperwork filed against it — the conversation with the manufacturer and NAFDAC proceeds from documents on both sides. A firm whose gate captures identities runs this in minutes; a firm whose gate waves trucks through runs it in weeks, in the newspapers.

Cost of capture, priced honestly. Identity capture is the slowest part of receiving, and clients push back. The consultant's answer is arithmetic: minutes per receipt against the recall that takes weeks, the warranty dispute that has no answer, the audit that cannot count. The premium is real; the coverage is the entire downstream edifice — and the flags were set at item creation (Buying 2) precisely so this desk has no discretion to skip it.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Rejections, quarantine & quality inspection
lessons.html:
Not everything on the truck deserves your shelves. The receipt's quality fork — accepted vs rejected, each with its warehouse — is how the gate says NO with a paper trail, and this chapter is its full operation.

The fork's mechanics. Each receipt row splits its counted quantity: Accepted Qty flows to the target warehouse as sellable (or usable) stock; Rejected Qty flows to the rejected warehouse — quarantine — where it is IN your possession but OUT of your sellable truth. Both movements happen at submission, both are valued, both are visible: the three damaged cartons exist, in quarantine, awaiting their fate, rather than existing nowhere (refused undocumented at the gate, then disputed from memory) or existing wrongly (waved into good stock to keep the queue moving — Chapter 9's conviction).

What gets rejected — the gate's standing rules, written. Transit damage (crushed, wet, broken seals); wrong goods (the substitution Procurement 4 warned about, caught with the truck still present); short-dated stock (under the firm's minimum-remaining-shelf-life rule for expiring goods — a POLICY number, not a mood); failed inspection (below). The rules live on paper at the desk, because a gate that rejects by individual judgment rejects inconsistently, and inconsistency is what suppliers negotiate against.

Quality inspection — the formal layer. Items flagged Inspection Required (on Purchase Receipt) demand a Quality Inspection before the receipt submits: a checklist document — parameters, readings, accept/reject verdict — per the item's template. The layer is proportionate by design: pharma actives, food lines, and safety-critical goods carry the flag; stationery does not. Where it applies, the inspection is the rejection's evidence: the verdict document, attached to the receipt, is what the supplier conversation and the NAFDAC file both cite. Inspections are honest only if performed — the pencil-whipped checklist (all boxes ticked at the desk without the goods opened) is worse than no layer, because it manufactures evidence of diligence that was not done.

The fate of quarantine. Rejected stock resolves on a clock, not by sedimentation: return to supplier (Chapter 6 — the usual fate, with the debit note as its money half); negotiated keep (the supplier discounts the damaged lot and it moves — deliberately, documented — to sellable or salvage); or write-off (disposal, documented, with the cost landing where the accountant directs). The weekly quarantine review — what is here, why, whose next step — is the small ritual that keeps the rejected warehouse a processing bay instead of a museum: quarantine that only fills is a warehouse of undecided money.

The supplier conversation. Every rejection is data with a name: rejection rates per supplier, by reason, per period — feeding the scorecard (Procurement 8) and the quarterly review. The supplier whose damage rate doubles has a packaging problem or a haulier problem; the one whose substitutions recur has a discipline problem; both conversations proceed from receipts, not recollections.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Landed cost: completing the truth of what things cost
lessons.html:
Procurement 2, Chapter 7 installed the THINKING — the invoice price is an ingredient, not the answer. This chapter installs the MECHANICS: how freight, duty, and clearing become part of received stock's valuation, so the numbers the firm trades on are the numbers reality charged.

The instrument: the Landed Cost Voucher. After (or alongside) the receipt, the voucher names: the purchase receipt(s) it applies to; the charges being added — each with its amount and its own supporting document (the freight invoice, the duty assessment, the clearing agent's bill, the haulage receipt); and the allocation basis spreading those charges across the received items — by value (the default logic: costlier items bear proportionally more) or by quantity (where handling cost tracks units, not worth). Submission does the arithmetic: each received item's valuation rises by its allocated share, and the stock ledger now carries units at their true landed figure.

What changes downstream — the whole point. Margin reports subtract the TRUE cost when selling ships these units; the import line's profitability is measured against reality instead of flattered by a factory price; Buying 2's viability pages reconcile against actuals (the estimated stack vs the voucher's actual stack — the variance is the import lane learning); and the accountant's P&L stops eating clearing costs as anonymous expenses while gross margin lies. The alternative — charges expensed into general buckets — was convicted in Procurement 2, Chapter 9 and stands convicted here with the fix in hand.

Timing and estimates. Charges arrive on their own schedules: freight billed at shipment, duty at clearing, the agent weeks later. The disciplines: voucher promptly per shipment as charges land (one shipment's stack in one or few vouchers, filed against its receipts — not a quarterly omnibus that no shipment can be reconciled from); and where goods must sell before the last bill arrives, the firm's policy on estimated charges (booked, then trued) is agreed WITH the accountant — the consultant's job is knowing the policy exists and encoding it, not inventing it per container.

The shipment file, completed. Procurement 1 opened the import documentation habit; here it closes: the receipt, the voucher, and every charge's paper filed together per shipment. The payoffs, restated as operations: the true cost of container X is a lookup; clearing-cost drift across shipments is visible (the agent whose fees crept 30% in a year is a negotiation, found by comparing vouchers); and the FX question — what did this container really cost in naira, and what does the next one cost at today's rate — is answered from records.

Scope discipline. Landed cost carries charges that attach to ACQUIRING the stock — freight, insurance, duty, clearing, inbound haulage. It does not become a dumping ground for general overheads, storage, or costs of running the warehouse; the accountant's line on what capitalises into stock is the line, and blurring it distorts valuation in the opposite direction from expensing. The instrument's power is precision; used loosely it just relocates the lie.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Returns to supplier
lessons.html:
Goods go back — the rejected lot, the recall pulled inward, the over-supply agreed away. The purchase return is Selling 5's return machinery with the direction reversed, and its properties are the same three no shortcut has.

The instrument. A purchase return is a Purchase Receipt with Is Return ticked, made against the original receipt, carrying negative quantities: submission moves stock OUT — from quarantine (the usual source: the rejected lot going home) or from good stock (the recall, the negotiated give-back) — written in the same ledger as everything else.

The three properties, inbound edition. Traceability: the return references the precise original receipt — which delivery, which PO, which serials or batch going back; the supplier's credit conversation proceeds from a document chain, not a dispute. Valuation: the return exits stock at the value it entered at — including its landed share where a voucher applied — so the ledger's cost truth survives the round trip; a bare stock adjustment guesses, and guesses compound. Identity: serials return by name, batches by lot — the biography records the exit, and the two-sided recall trail (Chapter 3) stays whole: B-204 arrived on this receipt, went back on this return.

The money half — named now, owned next module. The return receipt reverses STOCK; the supplier's ledger is corrected by the debit note — a return Purchase Invoice against the original — Procurement 7's Chapter. Hold the pairing as its sentence: stock reverses on the return receipt; money reverses on the debit note; one physical event, two ledgers, two linked documents — the exact mirror of the credit-note pairing you already hold from the selling side. What never substitutes: netting the return against the next delivery by handshake (two ledgers now disagree with one memory), or a supplier's verbal promise of credit (Chapter 9 meets what those promises age into).

Replacements. The supplier replaces the damaged lot: the replacement arrives as a NEW receipt against the PO (or its own agreed flow) — two movements, two documents, the identity trail showing the swap explicitly. Never an edit to the return, never no-paper because it netted out — fourth appearance of the two-movements law, and its last needed.

Logistics of the give-back. The physical return rides paper too: the supplier's collection reference or your outbound waybill recorded on the return document; quarantine's outflow reconciling to the return's quantities; and the weekly quarantine review (Chapter 4) confirming that what was resolved as return-to-supplier actually LEFT — the failure mode being goods written back to the supplier on paper while the pallets age in quarantine, which is a stock lie with a courtesy title.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The gate rules: tolerance, shortage & the unordered truck
lessons.html:
Three standing rules govern what the gate accepts, and each is policy-in-configuration rather than dock-side improvisation. This chapter is the three, plus the posture behind them.

Rule one — over-receipt tolerance. The mirror of Selling 4's over-delivery allowance: the receipt may exceed the PO's remaining quantity only within the item's over-receipt allowance (per item, global fallback — the Buying Settings number Procurement 8 owns). Within tolerance, the overage enters honestly and the row completes; beyond it, the receipt refuses to submit and the conversation happens with the truck present — accept formally (the PO amended or the policy's exception logged), or send the excess back on the spot. The policy logic transfers verbatim: zero tolerance for serialized goods (identity classes have no honest overage), a deliberate few percent for bulk (the 101st bag of cement blocks nobody), and never — the standing conviction — tolerance decided ad hoc at the dock.

Rule two — shortage is the PO's business, not the receipt's. The truck brings 160 against a remaining 180: the receipt records 160 — full stop. The 20 stays where it belongs: OPEN on the PO as remaining quantity, visible in the To-Receive views, chased by the expediting craft (Procurement 5) or short-closed and resourced when the supplier concedes. What the receipt never does: record 180 because the paperwork promised it (fiction at the gate), or quietly absorb the shortage by editing history. Short is short, on the document, with the supplier's delivery note annotated to match — the variance evidence the credit conversation will need.

Rule three — the unordered truck. Goods arrive that no PO ordered: the supplier's while we are delivering, we added..., the substitution beyond spec, the outright wrong consignment. The gate's answer is procedural, not personal: no PO, no receipt — unordered goods are not received into stock on dock-side goodwill, because a receipt without a commitment behind it has no rate, no match, no ancestry, and becomes an invoice dispute with your signature already on it. The paths that exist: refuse and send back (the default); or, where the addition is genuinely wanted, the commitment is created FIRST (a PO raised through whatever policy speed the situation merits — even an emergency PO is a document) and the receipt follows it. The rule's phrasing for the receiving team is one line: we receive against orders, not against trucks.

The posture beneath all three. The gate is where your firm's process meets other firms' improvisation, and the rules exist so the meeting is predictable: suppliers learn within weeks that overages need conversations, shortages get annotated, and unordered goods ride home — and their OWN dispatch discipline improves to match, because process at the gate is contagious in both directions. A gate that improvises trains the market to improvise at it.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: three arrivals at HealthTrade
lessons.html:
Three trucks, every chapter working. The threads continue from Procurement 5. Each step names its chapter.

Arrival one — Emzor drop one: 180 cartons (Ch. 1-4, 6). The receipt is created FROM the PO (pre-filled at the 300 remaining; edited to the drop's 180 — 2,160 units via the conversion). The count runs against the PO: 177 cartons sound, 3 crushed in transit. Batch capture: two lots on the truck — B-1147 (expiry 03/2028) and B-1152 (expiry 07/2028) — keyed from the physical cartons, quantities per lot; the remaining-shelf-life rule checks both against policy: pass. The receipt submits: 177 accepted to Central, 3 rejected to Quarantine, valuation written at the PO's ₦9,600. Emzor's delivery note is signed ANNOTATED: 180 counted, 3 damage-rejected. Within the week: the return receipt against this receipt — negative 3, batch-identified, quarantine outflow — with the debit note flagged to Procurement 7; Emzor's replacement 3 arrive days later as a NEW receipt. The PO ledger reads honestly throughout; the rejection enters Emzor's quality record (3/180 transit damage — a haulier conversation, not a crisis).

Arrival two — the chiller (Ch. 3, 4). Vendor A delivers on the revised committed date. Inspection Required is flagged on the item: the Quality Inspection runs its checklist — model against spec (the 350L confirmed; Procurement 4's substitution warning honoured at the last line of defence), power-on test, condition — verdict Accept, document attached. The serial CHL-2418839 is keyed from the unit's plate: its biography opens — received from Vendor A, this PO, this date, ₦1.395m — the record every future service call will read. Accepted to the Facilities store; the launch proceeds with paper behind it.

Arrival three — the import container (Ch. 2, 5). The Mumbai consignment clears in two stages; each stage is its own receipt from the PO at actual counted quantities, container and seal numbers recorded, batches and expiries keyed per lot. Then the Landed Cost Voucher: ocean freight (invoice attached), duty (assessment attached), clearing and terminal charges (agent's bill), haulage — allocated by value across the container's items. Valuations rise to true landed figures; the viability page's estimated stack reconciles against the voucher's actual (variance: clearing ran ₦180k over estimate — noted, and the agent's next bill will be compared). The shipment file closes complete: PO, receipts, voucher, every charge's paper — the container's true naira cost a permanent one-minute lookup.

The week's quarantine review (Ch. 4). One line only — Emzor's 3, already resolved as returned-and-replaced, outflow confirmed. The bay is a processing area, not a museum; the gate ends the week the way it started it: honest.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & support patterns
lessons.html:
The receiving gate's scar tissue — and inbound, the diseases are the ones that poison VALUATION and PROVENANCE, the two truths hardest to rebuild. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — "The receipt was submitted from the manifest; the count came later." Disease: fiction first, confession later (Ch. 2) — the ledger dictated by paperwork, corrected by embarrassment. Fix: submission follows the count, structurally — the document completed at the dock after verification; the manifest is the supplier's claim, not your record.

Pattern 2 — "The recall query returns nothing — but we definitely stocked that batch." Disease: batch capture skipped or keyed wrong at receipt (Ch. 3) — the identity was never born, so no downstream discipline can find it. Fix: reconstruct the affected window painfully once (supplier documentation against sales records); then capture-from-the-cartons as an audited gate rule — the recall that cannot run is the one that reaches the newspapers.

Pattern 3 — "Damaged goods are in sellable stock." Disease: the fork unused — rejects waved into good stock to keep the queue moving (Ch. 4). The damage surfaces at the customer, which is the most expensive place to discover it, with a return and a credit note now owed OUTBOUND. Fix: the rejected-warehouse fork as routine, the standing rejection rules at the desk, and the weekly quarantine review that proves the fork is being used.

Pattern 4 — "The import line looks profitable; the P&L disagrees." Disease: landed charges expensed while stock sits undervalued (Ch. 5) — Procurement 2's warning, now with the fix installed and skipped. Fix: the Landed Cost Voucher per shipment, charges papered and allocated; the viability pages reconciled against actuals.

Pattern 5 — "The supplier promised credit for the returns... in March." Disease: verbal-credit aging (Ch. 6) — stock went back on a handshake; no return receipt, no debit note, and the supplier's statement now disagrees with your memory. Fix: the pairing enforced — return receipt for the stock, debit note for the money (Procurement 7) — and the statement reconciliation (Procurement 1) that would have caught it at one month old.

Pattern 6 — "We accepted the extra pallets — they were already off the truck." Disease: the unordered truck received on goodwill (Ch. 7) — no rate, no match, no ancestry, and the invoice dispute arrives with your signature on the delivery note. Fix: we receive against orders, not against trucks — refuse, or paper the commitment first; the gate rules posted at the desk.

Pattern 7 — "Friday's arrivals were all posted Monday." Disease: posting-date batching (Ch. 1) — the chronology fictionalised for convenience; stock-as-at, valuation timing, and dispute evidence all read a weekend that never happened. Fix: post at possession; the governance version of date adjustments belongs to accounting policy, not dock convenience — the same law as the outbound gate, because it is the same ledger.

The law. Procurement 1: purchase documents are downstream of supplier masters. Procurement 2: cost truth begins at the item. Procurement 3: the request layer separates need from commitment. Procurement 4: sourcing is a decision record. Procurement 5: the PO is the single source of inbound truth. This module adds the sixth: the receiving gate is where the world enters the system — keep it honest, and every valuation, every recall, every match downstream can be believed. Count before signing, capture identities from the goods, fork the damaged, land the true cost, return with paper, and receive against orders. A firm whose gate holds these disciplines trusts its own shelves; a firm whose gate improvises audits them forever.

purchase_invoice.title: Procurement 7 — Purchase Invoices, Payments & the Nigerian Frame
purchase_invoice.desc: The cash-out module: the liability event, the three-way match armed, payable terms engineering, the controlled payment run, supplier advances, WHT as the withholding agent with remittance discipline, input VAT and the 21st, and debit notes with the correction doctrine.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Purchase Invoice as the liability event
lessons.html:
Selling 7 taught the invoice as the accounting event, money-in. The Purchase Invoice is its mirror: the document whose submission books the supplier's claim as your liability — the payable to the supplier, the expense or stock-received value, and the input VAT asset (Chapter 7) — dated by its posting date, due by its terms. When any question begins when do the books recognise what we owe…, the answer is: at purchase-invoice submission. Nothing before it owes money; nothing after it changes what is owed except payment and the debit note.

Creation paths, chosen by flow:

  • From the Purchase Receipt — the standard route in goods trade: billing exactly what was possessed. Quantities arrive as received quantities; the receipt advances toward its billed completion; and — decisively — the invoice is born PRE-MATCHED to possession, which is half the three-way match (Chapter 2) done by construction.
  • From the Purchase Order — the advance-billing flows: the import deposit invoiced before shipment, milestone billing on services. The PO's billed ledger counts up while received sits behind it, and the To-Receive status keeps the physical claim visible after finance has moved (Procurement 5, Chapter 4).
  • Standalone — legitimate for genuinely document-less spend (utilities, statutory payments, services the policy exempted from the PO layer) and SUSPICIOUS everywhere else: a standalone invoice in goods trade matches nothing, closes nothing, and is precisely the shape supplier fraud and duplicate billing arrive in. The policy line from Procurement 3 applies: which spend categories may bill standalone is WRITTEN, and the rest go through the chain.

The Update Stock trap, inbound. An invoice with Update Stock ticked moves inventory IN itself — legitimate only where the flow deliberately has no Purchase Receipt (small direct-to-shelf supplies per policy). Ticked on an invoice made after a receipt already moved the goods, stock enters TWICE — the inbound twin of Selling 7's double-deduction, producing phantom surplus instead of phantom shortage, and just as capable of poisoning a stocktake. The rule transfers verbatim: where Update Stock is on, there is no receipt in that flow at all.

Two dates, permanently distinct. The posting date is when the books record the liability — honest to when the claim was accepted, feeding the correct VAT month (Chapter 7) and the correct expense period. The due date is when payment falls due — computed from terms (Chapter 3), never typed. Conflating them is the root of AP-ageing confusion exactly as it was for AR, and the cure is the same engineering, mirrored.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The three-way match, armed
lessons.html:
Every module in this track has been quietly building one control, and this chapter fires it. The three-way match holds the supplier's claim against two documents your own firm wrote, and pays only what all three agree on. It is the single cheapest auditor a trading company can employ, and it works precisely because each leg was kept honest upstream.

The three legs. The Purchase Order — what was COMMITTED: quantities, and rates that are agreed prices or competed quotations (Procurement 4-5), protected from bending by the rate-amendment conviction (Procurement 5, Chapter 6). The Purchase Receipt — what was POSSESSED: counted at the gate, shortages recorded, rejections forked (Procurement 6). The Purchase Invoice — what is CLAIMED. The match asks two questions of every invoice line: does the claimed QUANTITY exceed what was received and not yet billed? does the claimed RATE exceed what was committed? Agreement books the liability; disagreement stops the line and names its variance.

The variance taxonomy — each with its resolution:

  • Quantity variance — invoiced 180, received 177 (the damaged 3): the honest resolutions are the supplier invoicing the received quantity, or invoicing 180 WITH the 3-carton debit note standing against it (Chapter 8) — the pair netting true. What never resolves it: booking 180 because the paper says so; the receipt counted, and the count governs.
  • Price variance — invoiced ₦9,850 against a committed ₦9,600: the DISPUTE path (the invoice held, the supplier queried against the standing rate — usually a their-side error or an unencoded price move, and either way the committed rate is the negotiating floor), or the documented-renegotiation path where the change is genuinely agreed (papered, encoded to the buying list, THEN booked). Never the amendment path — Procurement 5's conviction, now at its point of enforcement.
  • The unmatched invoice — a claim with no receipt behind it: goods trade's loudest alarm. Either the receipt is missing (the gate skipped — fix the record before the payment) or the goods never came (the claim is air). Booking it anyway is paying for possession you cannot show — Chapter 10's Pattern 1, and the fraud shape the match exists to catch.

Tolerances, deliberately. Kobo-level rounding and configured small variances pass without ceremony — the match is a control, not a harassment engine, and the firm's variance tolerance (a policy number, like every gate number in this track) keeps it proportionate. Above tolerance, the line stops, and the STOP is the feature: the conversation happens before the money moves, which is the entire economics of the control — a disputed invoice costs an email; a recovered overpayment costs a campaign.

The match queue as routine. Procurement 5 named the To-Bill list the match queue; here is its operation: receipts awaiting invoices worked oldest-first as claims arrive, each invoice entered FROM its receipt (born pre-matched), variances resolved by the taxonomy, and the queue's age watched both ways — your unbooked liabilities and their lagging invoices (the statement-reconciliation thread from Procurement 1 closing the loop monthly). A firm that runs this queue pays exactly what it owes, knows exactly what it owes, and can prove both — which is the whole module in one sentence.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Payable terms & due-date engineering
lessons.html:
Selling 7 engineered the dates money comes IN; this chapter mirrors it for money going OUT — because the payables posture Procurement 1 preached (pay well, deliberately) is executable only if due dates are computed truth.

The inheritance chain, payable-side. Terms flow supplier master → purchase order → purchase invoice: the Net-30 negotiated at onboarding (Procurement 1, Chapter 4 — the credit line procurement built) computes each invoice's due date from its posting date. Multi-portion templates serve staged supplier deals exactly as they served staged customer deals: the import's 30%-advance/70%-against-documents is a terms template whose portions age independently — the deposit due now, the balance due at its trigger — and retentions YOU hold on contractor invoices (the 10% until commissioning) are the last portion aging as not-yet-due, the mirror of the retention you charged Montaigne.

The AP ageing, operated. With computed due dates, the Accounts Payable report's buckets mean something, and Procurement 1's reading posture becomes a weekly routine: due-this-week is the funding list (cash scheduled against it — treasury's input); coming-due is the planning view; overdue is the explain-personally list — each entry a promise breaking, called BEFORE the supplier calls, with a date attached (the deliberate-loan discipline: taken with a call, never defaulted into). The right-hand columns of AP are your firm's reputation aging in public.

Early-payment discounts, evaluated not assumed. Suppliers offer them — 2% for payment in 10 days against Net-30. The evaluation is arithmetic, not enthusiasm: the discount's annualised return against the firm's cost of cash (2% for 20 days early is a very high annualised rate — usually worth taking when cash allows; a thin discount for long acceleration is not), decided as policy per supplier or per offer, and executed through the run (Chapter 4) so the discount is actually captured — the offer accepted in spirit and missed in practice, paying full after the window, is the worst of both.

Terms renegotiation as treasury work, continued. The payment behaviour this chapter operationalises IS the evidence for Procurement 1's terms-extension path: the account that never slips earns Net-15 → Net-30 → Net-45 over trust's timetable, and the record of on-time runs is the negotiation exhibit. Meanwhile the credit-limit mirror applies in reverse: as YOUR terms lengthen, the supplier is carrying more of your float — expect their own risk eye on your account, and keep the statement reconciliation (Procurement 1, Chapter 5) current so the relationship's numbers never surprise either side.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The payment run: money out, controlled
lessons.html:
Money leaves through the Payment Entry — and on the buy side, HOW it leaves is a control surface, because outbound payment is where the firm's cash meets the world's fraud. This chapter is the entry's craft plus the run's governance.

The entry, mirrored. One real-world payment = one Payment Entry: the ₦12m transfer settling four Emzor invoices is ONE entry with four allocation rows; three separate transfers are three entries. Entries mirror bank lines — the reconciliation law, verbatim from Selling 7, because it is the same bank statement read from the other side. The fields carry the same weight: mode, paid-from account (the actual bank debited — month-end matching lives here), reference (your transfer reference, recorded at execution), and the allocation rows naming which invoices this payment settles — oldest first by default, adjusted where specific invoices are being settled, and always TOLD to the supplier: the remittance advice you send is the mirror of the one you demanded from customers, and it is what keeps two firms' ledgers allocating identically (their unapplied-payment confusion is your reconciliation debt).

The run as a controlled batch. Payments go out in scheduled RUNS — weekly is the common rhythm — not as a dribble of individual urgencies, and the run's structure IS the control set:

  • Selection: due-this-week from the AP ageing, plus captured early-payment discounts (Chapter 3), plus resolved disputes — a LIST, reviewable, before anything moves.
  • Verification: every payee's bank details from the MASTER's verified fields (Procurement 1, Chapter 3's out-of-band rule) — never from details riding the invoice, never from an email received this week. This is the point in the entire track where the payment-fraud control actually executes: the lookalike-domain email asking to redirect payment dies here or nowhere, because the run pays masters, not messages.
  • Approval: the run reviewed and released by someone other than its preparer — the two-pairs-of-eyes that costs minutes and is the difference between an attempted fraud and a successful one. Sized to the firm: in an 11-person company this is the accountant preparing and the MD releasing; the principle, not the org chart, is the requirement.
  • Execution and recording: payments executed, references captured onto the entries same-day, advices sent. An executed-but-unrecorded run is cash in flight that the ledger cannot see — the reconciliation break built by hand.

Urgency, governed. True urgent payments exist; the governance is that they run through the SAME verification and approval at higher speed — an urgent path, not an exception to control. The email whose whole design is too urgent for the usual checks has told you what it is. (Chapter 10 meets the firm that learned this by wire transfer.)

What never pays suppliers: bare journal entries (references, modes, and allocations orphaned — the Selling 7 conviction, mirrored), personal transfers reimbursed later (the audit hole with a kind face), and cash outside the recorded modes. The payment ledger is believed exactly as far as every naira out has an entry, a reference, and an allocation.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Supplier advances & allocation
lessons.html:
Money before goods is normal in Nigerian procurement — the import deposit, the mobilisation payment, the advance the new supplier demands before trust exists. Selling 7 taught the machinery from the receiving side; this chapter runs it paying, and the black hole threatens in mirror image.

The advance out. A Payment Entry against the supplier with no invoice reference: the amount sits as YOUR unallocated credit on THEIR account — visible in the supplier's balance, reducing net payable exposure, waiting. It is not an expense (nothing has been consumed), not a receipt of goods (nothing has arrived), and not unrecorded cash-in-flight (the entry exists the day the money moves, referenced, from the run's controls like any payment).

Allocation — the advance meets its invoice. The supplier's invoice lands (through the match, Chapter 2 — advances change nothing about matching discipline); the advance is allocated against it, netting the payable down; the balance, if any, pays by its terms. The import flow in miniature: 30% deposit paid against the PO (entry, unallocated); shipment documents arrive; the invoice books through the match; the deposit allocates; the 70% balance schedules by its terms portion. Every naira's position is readable at every stage — which is the entire point.

The mirror black hole. Selling 7's disease was advances RECEIVED and never allocated — customers dunned for money already sent. The payable mirror: advances PAID and never allocated — the supplier's invoice settled in full by a fresh payment while your deposit sits forgotten as credit, and the firm has paid twice, discoverable only by the supplier's honesty or your reconciliation. The prevention is the same monthly read, both directions now: unallocated credits per supplier — each one matched to its invoice, refund-claimed, or explained. The statement reconciliation (Procurement 1, Chapter 5) is the backstop that catches what the read misses, at one month old instead of at year-end.

Refunds from suppliers. The deal dies after the deposit — the import cancelled, the contract terminated: the supplier refunds, and the refund is a payment IN against the supplier, consuming the credit, referenced and mirrored in the bank like every other movement. The alternatives age badly: the credit left to apply against future business without written agreement is a loan you did not mean to make, and the verbal we will sort it out is Procurement 6's handshake disease wearing a finance costume. Deposits into failed deals are chased with the same politeness and persistence as receivables — because that is exactly what they have become.

Advances and the match. One discipline worth stating explicitly: an advance never SUBSTITUTES for the match. The deposit paid does not oblige booking whatever invoice eventually arrives — the claim still matches against commitment and possession, and a variance on an advance-backed invoice resolves by the same taxonomy, with the advance simply waiting on the correct final figure. Money forward does not mean scrutiny waived.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — WHT: your firm as the withholding agent
lessons.html:
Selling 7, Chapter 6 taught withholding tax from the receiving end — your customers deducting from you. Procurement completes the symmetry, and the stakes rise: as the PAYER, your firm is the withholding agent, and the obligations are now yours to execute, remit, and evidence. This is the chapter Nigerian practice demands and generic training never writes.

The mechanics, precisely. Paying a qualifying supplier for services or contracts, the firm deducts WHT at the rate the supplier's classification sets — Supplier Type is the rate class (companies and individuals withhold at different rates; the schedule of rates and covered transaction types is the accountant's domain, encoded once), which is why Procurement 1 made the type field a tax fact and the TIN mandatory at onboarding. The payment mathematics on a ₦1,000,000 qualifying service invoice at 5%: the supplier receives ₦950,000; the invoice is settled in full — the Payment Entry allocates ₦1,000,000, with a ₦50,000 deduction row posting to the WHT PAYABLE liability account. Note the mirror exactly: receiving WHT built a receivable ASSET (tax paid on your behalf, creditable); withholding WHT builds a payable LIABILITY (tax you now hold for FIRS, remittable). Same instrument, opposite ledger sides, and confusing them misstates both.

The remittance discipline. The WHT payable account accumulates the month's withholdings; remittance to FIRS follows on the statutory schedule — with the return identifying each supplier by TIN and amount. The operating rhythm: the account reconciled monthly against the deduction entries (every naira withheld traceable to its payment and its supplier), remitted on time — because withheld-but-unremitted tax is the worst liability a firm can carry: it is not your money, the penalties and interest for late remittance compound, and it is the finding that turns a routine FIRS visit hostile (Chapter 10's pattern names it the black hole with teeth).

The evidence — now yours to issue. The supplier will chase their credit evidence exactly as you chased Montaigne's certificate — because to them it is creditable tax, real money once papered. The discipline mirrors what you demanded: deductions logged per supplier, evidence issued promptly with the remittance's references, the supplier's accounts contact (Procurement 1's people layer) knowing where to ask. A firm that withholds cleanly and evidences promptly is the counterparty every serious supplier prefers — the payables version of paying well.

Scope judgment. What attracts WHT (services, contracts, rents, and the scheduled categories) versus what does not (typically pure goods-for-resale transactions) is a classification question the accountant owns and the consultant encodes — per supplier and per transaction type, so the deduction fires where it should and never where it should not. Both errors cost: failing to withhold where required leaves YOUR firm liable for the tax it should have deducted; withholding where not required short-pays a supplier lawfully owed in full and manufactures a dispute. The configuration conversation at implementation is exactly these two lists, written, with the accountant's sign-off — and the HealthTrade case (Chapter 9) shows the Individual-type clearing agent's invoice running the full cycle.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Input VAT & the 21st, completed
lessons.html:
Selling 6 taught the output side: VAT collected, held, filed by the 21st. This chapter completes the return: the input VAT on your purchases is a claimable asset, and its capture discipline is a cash discipline.

The mechanics. The purchase tax template on POs and invoices computes input VAT to its asset account — the mirror of the output liability. The monthly filing NETS them: output collected minus input claimable equals the remittance (or the credit position). Every properly captured purchase invoice therefore reduces the month's cash remittance naira-for-naira up to the output collected — which reframes input-VAT hygiene from compliance chore to money recovery: unclaimable input VAT is a donation, made monthly, in silence.

What makes input VAT claimable. The claim stands on its paper: a proper tax invoice from a VAT-registered supplier — their registration verified at onboarding (Procurement 1's master fields earning again), the invoice itself compliant (and, as the FIRS e-invoicing regime extends, validated through the pipeline your NGE Portal serves — the architecture argument from Selling 6 running in reverse: template-driven purchase documents produce claimable input as a by-product). The capture disciplines: the correct purchase tax template on every document (defaulted from the supplier — set once); VAT posted to the input account, never lost inside item rates or expense lines (the inbound twin of the typed-VAT disease); and the invoice booked in its correct month (Chapter 1's posting-date honesty deciding WHICH return the claim lands in).

The monthly reconciliation, both sides now. Selling 6 reconciled the output account to the sales register; the complete pre-filing routine reconciles BOTH: output account to sales invoices, input account to purchase invoices — every naira in each account traceable to a document, discrepancies resolved before the 21st, the filing figure read from accounts that have already proven themselves. The firm with this routine files in an hour and answers FIRS queries from printouts; the firm without it reconstructs each month under deadline, badly.

The classification edges. Not all input VAT is claimable against all output — exempt-supply businesses and mixed traders face apportionment rules that are the accountant's terrain; and purchases from unregistered suppliers carry no claimable VAT at all, which quietly PRICES those suppliers higher than their invoices suggest (a ₦100 invoice with claimable ₦7.5 input beats a ₦99 invoice with none — arithmetic worth teaching every buyer, and a legitimate line in Procurement 4's comparison discipline). The consultant's role at the edges is the standing one: know the questions, encode the accountant's answers, and never improvise tax classification per document.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Debit notes & the correction doctrine
lessons.html:
Submitted purchase invoices are never edited — the immutability that makes the ledger evidence, now protecting the payables side. Reversal and correction run through the debit note, and the doctrine transfers from Selling 7 with the roles reversed.

The instrument. A debit note is a Purchase Invoice with Is Return ticked, made against the original invoice, carrying negative amounts: the payable reduced, the expense or stock value reversed, the input VAT reversed — each by the credited quantities and values, each linked to what it unwinds. The original flips to Debit-Note-Issued status; the note carries Return; two documents, permanently married.

The two occasions, mirrored:

  • Returned goods — the money half of Procurement 6's pairing, now executed: stock went back on the return receipt; the debit note gives the money its mirror — raised against the original invoice for the returned quantities, partial returns getting partial notes, the linkage keeping every remainder honest. The pairing sentence, final form: stock reverses on the return receipt; money reverses on the debit note; one physical event, two ledgers, two linked documents — and the supplier's corresponding credit note should MEET your debit note in the monthly statement reconciliation, the two firms' paper agreeing because both were written.
  • Billing corrections — the overcharge that slipped the match, the duplicate invoice discovered, the post-booking price resolution: debit note against the wrong invoice, then the correct invoice booked (or the balance simply reduced, where the correction is the whole story). Both documents stand forever — the claim that was booked AND the visible instrument that unwound it — which is what your own auditor and any FIRS review of the input-VAT trail expect to find. The convicted alternatives are the same convicts: journals quietly patching payables, administrative edits to submitted invoices — a payables ledger that can be silently corrected proves nothing, including your innocence.

What your firm does with the credit. Two lawful endings, chosen commercially: the credit applies against other invoices (the next run nets it — the usual fate in a continuing relationship) or is refunded by the supplier (a payment in, referenced, banked — Chapter 5's machinery). The credit is a first-class balance until one ending consumes it: never an off-ledger IOU, never they will remember at the next order — Procurement 6's verbal-credit disease, cured here at the money layer.

Governance, mirrored. Debit notes erase payables, so they carry the visibility posture: the monthly read by value, reason, and supplier. A boring report means receiving and matching are accurate; a spike is quality upstream (returns — route to the supplier conversation and the scorecard) or claims discipline inside (corrections — route to the match's tolerance and training). Either way the report knew first — the sentence is Selling 7's verbatim, because the mirror is exact.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study: the HealthTrade money month
lessons.html:
Every thread from Procurement 3-6 now settles to zero. One month of payables, every chapter clocking in.

Thread one — Emzor, matched and settled (Ch. 1-2, 8). Emzor's invoice arrives for drop one: 180 cartons at ₦9,600. The invoice is entered FROM the receipt — which received 177 accepted, 3 rejected-and-returned. The match flags the quantity variance; the resolution is the documented pair: the 180-carton invoice booked WITH the 3-carton debit note standing against it (raised against the invoice, linked to the return receipt — the pairing complete), netting the payable to 177 × ₦9,600. Drop two's invoice (80 cartons) matches clean against its receipt. Emzor's monthly statement, reconciled per Procurement 1's routine, shows their credit note meeting your debit note — two firms' paper agreeing.

Thread two — the price variance caught (Ch. 2). The backup distributor's invoice for the 40-carton gap arrives at ₦9,850… per carton, plus a ₦120-per-carton 'fuel surcharge' nobody agreed. The match stops the line: the committed rate is the scoped ₦9,850, full stop. The dispute email cites the PO; the supplier corrects the invoice in two days; the corrected claim books clean. Cost of the control: one email. Value: ₦4,800 this once — and the supplier's education that this customer's match runs, which is worth more than the ₦4,800 every month after.

Thread three — the import deposit allocated (Ch. 5). The Mumbai balance falls due against documents: the invoice books through the match (quantities per the receipts, rate per the PO, the landed voucher having done valuation separately — Procurement 6); the 30% advance allocates; the 70% balance schedules per its terms portion and enters next week's run. The unallocated-credits read at month-end shows zero forgotten deposits — the mirror black hole, empty.

Thread four — WHT withheld and remitted (Ch. 6). The clearing agent's service invoice — ₦400,000, Individual type (Procurement 1's onboarding fact now computing money) — runs the agent cycle: payment entry allocates the full ₦400,000, receives ₦380,000 to the agent, and posts ₦20,000 to the WHT payable. Month-end: the WHT payable reconciles to its deduction entries, the remittance files against the agent's TIN on schedule, and the evidence issues to the agent's accounts contact — who thanks you, because most of their customers make them chase it.

Thread five — the run (Ch. 3-4). Friday's run: due-this-week from the ageing (the chiller's Net-15 invoice among them — matched at award-exact ₦1.395m, Vendor A's details from the verified master), one early-payment discount captured where the arithmetic cleared the bar, the corrected backup-distributor invoice, the Mumbai balance. Prepared by the accountant, released by the MD, references recorded same-day, advices sent naming the allocations. Mid-week, an urgent email arrives from a lookalike domain asking to redirect a payment: it dies against the run's rule — masters, not messages — exactly as its predecessor died at onboarding (Procurement 1's case), and for the same reason: the control is boring, and it held.

Month-end (Ch. 7). Output and input VAT accounts both reconcile to their registers; the netting computes the remittance; the filing takes the hour it should. The month's ledger of spend: every naira out matched to commitment and possession, every deduction remitted and evidenced, every advance allocated, every credit papered — and not one number living in anyone's memory. The mirror of Montaigne's zero, achieved from the paying chair.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Support patterns & the seventh law
lessons.html:
The cash-out module's scar tissue — the most expensive tickets on the buying side, because every disease here is money leaving wrongly or obligations compounding quietly. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — invoices booked and paid with no receipt behind them. Disease: the match bypassed or never armed (Ch. 2) — paying for possession the firm cannot show; the shape duplicate billing and supplier fraud arrive in. Fix: the match as structural routine — invoices entered from receipts, unmatched claims quarantined until their receipt exists or the claim dies; and the standalone-invoice policy list enforced.

Pattern 2 — "the match kept blocking things, so we relaxed it during the rush." Disease: control eroded under pressure (Ch. 2) — and the overcharges that arrived during the relaxation are now archaeology. Fix: tolerances tuned (a proportionate match does not block honest trade), the urgent path SPEEDING the control instead of skipping it, and the erosion treated as governance — the same escalation as every evidence-destruction pattern in both tracks.

Pattern 3 — withheld-but-unremitted WHT accumulating. Disease: the black hole with teeth (Ch. 6) — deductions taken, remittance drifting, penalties compounding on money that was never yours. Fix: the monthly reconcile-and-remit rhythm with a named owner; the arrears regularised with the accountant leading; and the standing truth taught — WHT payable is FIRS's money in your custody, the one liability that never benefits from aging.

Pattern 4 — input VAT lost. Disease: the silent donation (Ch. 7) — wrong templates, VAT buried in expense lines, invoices from unverified suppliers, claims booked in wrong months. Fix: templates defaulted from masters, the monthly input-account-to-register reconcile, supplier VAT registration in the onboarding gate — and the recovered remittance reduction as the fix's own business case.

Pattern 5 — the double payment. Disease: the mirror black hole (Ch. 5) — the advance never allocated, the invoice paid fresh, the deposit forgotten. Fix: the monthly unallocated read both directions, allocation at invoice-booking as routine, and the statement reconciliation as backstop; the recovery call to the supplier is honest and usually successful — theirs would be too.

Pattern 6 — payments outside the run to urgent instructions. Disease: the control skipped at exactly the moment it existed for (Ch. 4) — the lookalike email, the changed account details, the too-urgent-to-verify wire. Fix — usually after a painful recovery attempt — is absolute: masters not messages, verification out-of-band, the urgent path through the same gates faster, no exceptions BECAUSE of urgency. The fraud's entire design is the exception.

Pattern 7 — supplier credits living in memory. Disease: the verbal-credit ledger (Ch. 8; Procurement 6's Pattern 5 at the money layer) — returns netted by handshake, promises aging, statements disagreeing by amounts nobody can reconstruct. Fix: the pairing enforced (return receipt + debit note, always), credits as first-class balances consumed by application or refund, and the monthly statement reconciliation where your debit notes and their credit notes meet in writing.

The seventh law — and the track nearly complete. Procurement 1: purchase documents are downstream of supplier masters. Procurement 2: cost truth begins at the item. Procurement 3: the request layer separates need from commitment. Procurement 4: sourcing is a decision record. Procurement 5: the PO is the single source of inbound truth. Procurement 6: the receiving gate is where the world enters the system. This module: the purchase ledger is the spend truth — pay only what was ordered, received, and claimed in agreement; the three-way match is the firm's cheapest auditor, and it only works because every upstream module kept its leg honest. One module remains: the advanced layer that makes all of it structure.
